A text simulator, not an assistant; three concrete failure ways.

recall.question: What does pre-training actually optimize?
recall.answer: Next-token prediction: the probability distribution of what comes next in internet text.

keyTerms.definition: Supervised fine-tuning: show the shape of the job by example.
What SFT is; works where demos cover the behavior.

recall.question: What is SFT, mechanically?
recall.answer: The simplest post-training step; which tokens get loss and why.

recall.question: Why is quality more important than quantity in SFT data?

sections.title: 3. Preference data: the fuel everything runs on

keyTerms.definition: Rankings, not absolute scores; the fuel for chapters 4-6.
Why practitioners say it in RLHF.

recall.question: Why rankings instead of absolute scores?
recall.answer: Comparisons are the human signal SFT cannot give: which of two good answers is better.

sections.title: 4. The RLHF pipeline end to end: reward model, then PPO

keyTerms.definition: Turns comparisons into scores; Bradley-Terry scalar head.
Proximal policy optimization; the clipped objective with KL penalty.
Keeps the policy near the SFT model; stops drift.

recall.question: What are the three RLHF stages?
recall.answer: Train a reward model from comparisons, optimize the policy with PPO, KL leash to the SFT model.

recall.question: Why the clip and the KL penalty?
recall.answer: The clip bounds the update; the KL penalty stops drift from the reference.

sections.title: 5. DPO (Direct Preference Optimization), derived from first principles

keyTerms.definition: Direct Preference Optimization: the RLHF closed-form optimum as a classification loss.
Do not skip it in the derivation.

recall.question: Where did the reward model go?
recall.answer: Pure algebra absorbs it; the chapter asks what assumptions you smuggled in.

recall.question: When does DPO beat PPO, and when does it fail?
recall.answer: The chapter's design prompt; no rollouts versus online exploration.

sections.title: 6. GRPO and RLVR: RL with checkable answers

keyTerms.definition: RL with verifiable rewards; no human preference data needed.
Group-relative policy optimization; advantages from a group, no critic.
Replaces the learned reward model where answers are checkable.

recall.question: Why does RLVR not need human preference data?
recall.answer: Math and code are checkable: right-or-wrong beats preferred.

keyTerms.definition: The model labels itself guided by a written constitution; two phases.
Written principles guiding the model’s self-labeling.

recall.question: Is the constitution a system prompt?
recall.answer: The chapter's design prompt; why or why not.

recall.question: What do humans still have to do?
recall.answer: Write the constitution; the model does the labeling.

sections.title: 8. Reward hacking: when the proxy eats the goal

keyTerms.definition: The policy learns to score well instead of be good.
Demos, preferences, reward models, constitutions; all proxies.

recall.question: Your reward climbs but human evals are flat. What do you do?
recall.answer: Suspect reward hacking; the proxy ate the goal.

recall.question: What failure do chapters 2-7 share?
recall.answer: Each optimizes a proxy: demos, preferences, reward models, constitutions.
